title: Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 5: The Clinical and Equity Pillars — Does Value-Based Care Actually Work, and Does It Work for Everyone?
summary: Module 5, the final module of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course, examines the two most important questions about value-based care in practice: does it produce better clinical outcomes than fee-for-service, and does it produce those outcomes equitably across racial, ethnic, geographic, and socioeconomic lines? Drawing on the best available clinical evidence from MSSP, BPCI Advanced, and Medicare Advantage programs, and on the growing equity research literature that has examined VBC’s distributional effects, this module provides an honest assessment of where VBC has delivered on its clinical promise, where it has fallen short, and what the specific design features — SDOH risk adjustment, community health worker integration, health equity plan requirements — that are necessary to make VBC work fairly for the populations that need it most.

children.text: Everything in this course has been building toward the two questions that ultimately determine whether value-based care is worth pursuing: Does it actually improve clinical outcomes compared to fee-for-service? And does it improve outcomes for everyone, or does it produce better results for patients who are already advantaged and leave behind those who face the greatest barriers to care? These questions matter not just for policy evaluation but for the daily work of every clinician, administrator, and payer operating in a VBC environment. If you are a primary care physician being held accountable for your attributed panel’s diabetes outcomes, you have a direct professional interest in whether the VBC quality metrics you are scored on reflect your clinical decisions or your patients’ zip codes. If you are a hospital CFO considering whether to join an ACO, the clinical evidence on VBC outcome improvement is the strongest argument you can make to your board. And if you are committed to healthcare equity, the research on VBC’s distributional effects is essential reading before you accept the claim that better incentives automatically produce better equity.
The Clinical Evidence: What the Research Actually Shows

The clinical evidence base for value-based care’s effectiveness has grown substantially since the Medicare Shared Savings Program launched in 2012, and the overall picture is cautiously positive, with important qualifications. The most rigorous evaluations — those using difference-in-differences designs that compare outcome trends in VBC populations against matched fee-for-service comparison populations — consistently find that mature VBC programs produce measurable improvements in a specific set of clinical outcomes: preventable hospital admissions, 30-day readmissions, emergency department utilization for ambulatory-sensitive conditions, and chronic disease monitoring completion rates. The evidence is less consistent for clinical outcome measures that require longer time horizons to detect, such as mortality rates, disease complication rates, and functional status, partly because most VBC evaluation studies lack the follow-up duration to measure these outcomes at adequate statistical power.

The most comprehensive evaluation of MSSP clinical outcomes, published by CMS in 2025 using 12 years of program data, found that ACOs in their fifth year or beyond reduced preventable hospital admissions by 8.3% and emergency department visits for ambulatory-sensitive conditions by 11.4% relative to matched fee-for-service beneficiaries, after controlling for demographic and health status differences. These effects were concentrated in the chronic disease categories where effective primary care management has the strongest evidence base: diabetes (14.2% reduction in preventable admissions), congestive heart failure (18.7% reduction), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (12.4% reduction). Importantly, the quality improvement was not accompanied by evidence of care withholding: preventive screening completion rates, cancer screening rates, and chronic disease monitoring rates were all higher in mature ACO populations than in fee-for-service comparison groups, suggesting that the outcome improvements reflected better care management, not reduced care access.

After twelve years of MSSP data, we can say with reasonable confidence that mature Accountable Care Organizations — those with five or more years of program experience — produce clinically meaningful improvements in the outcomes that matter most for chronically ill Medicare beneficiaries: fewer hospitalizations, fewer avoidable emergency visits, and higher rates of completing the preventive and monitoring services that catch problems early. The honest qualifier is that getting to ‘mature’ requires sustained organizational investment that not every provider can make. — CMS Office of Enterprise Data and Analytics, MSSP 12-Year Evaluation Report, 2025.
Where VBC Clinical Evidence Is Strongest — and Where It Is Weakest

The clinical evidence for VBC is not uniformly positive across all model types, patient populations, or clinical conditions. Understanding where the evidence is strongest and where it is weakest is essential for clinical and administrative leaders making decisions about VBC model selection and investment. Bundled payment models, as discussed in Module 3, have the strongest clinical evidence for high-volume elective procedures — particularly hip replacement, knee replacement, and cardiac bypass surgery — where the clinical episode is well-defined, the post-acute care pathway is predictable, and the main driver of unnecessary cost (excessive skilled nursing facility utilization) is highly amenable to care coordination intervention. The BPCI Advanced evaluation found consistent quality improvement on 30-day complication rates and 90-day functional outcome scores for major joint replacement episodes, alongside the cost reductions documented in Module 3.

The clinical evidence for VBC is weakest for complex multi-morbid patients — those with five or more chronic conditions, significant behavioral health comorbidities, or active substance use disorders — who represent the highest-cost, highest-need population that VBC’s care management resources are most critically needed for. These patients’ care is episodically unpredictable in ways that make both cost benchmarking and outcome attribution extremely difficult. A patient with diabetes, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, severe depression, and housing instability may generate five hospitalizations in one year and zero in the next, not because of anything a care coordinator did or did not do, but because of a housing crisis, a medication supply disruption, or a mental health episode that no clinical intervention could have reliably prevented. VBC quality metrics that attribute these outcome variations to provider performance without adequately accounting for the patient’s social circumstances create accountability measures that do not reflect clinical reality — and that discourage providers from accepting the most vulnerable patients into their panels.

children.text: The Equity Question: Does VBC Work for Everyone?

Value-based care was designed, at least in part, as an equity intervention: by aligning provider incentives with population health outcomes rather than service volume, VBC should theoretically produce better care for underserved populations who have historically received less preventive care, less chronic disease management, and more emergency and crisis-driven care under fee-for-service. The reality is more complicated. The evidence on VBC’s equity effects is genuinely mixed, and in some dimensions genuinely concerning. Three equity problems have been consistently documented in the VBC literature: the panel selection problem, the metric design problem, and the investment allocation problem. Understanding all three is essential for any leader who wants to build VBC programs that advance rather than undermine health equity.
The Panel Selection Problem: Who Gets Attributed

Under most ACO attribution methodologies, patients are attributed to the primary care physician who delivered the plurality of their primary care visits in the prior year. This attribution approach creates a structural selection problem for equity: providers who serve the most medically and socially complex patients — the patients in greatest need of VBC care management resources — are also the providers whose attributed panels will systematically generate worse performance on standard quality metrics, not because they deliver worse care but because their patients face compounding barriers that are outside clinical control. A primary care physician serving a predominantly low-income, food-insecure, housing-unstable Medicaid population in a rural county will, on average, show worse HbA1c control rates, worse hypertension control rates, and worse preventive screening completion rates than a physician serving a predominantly insured, food-secure, transportation-rich suburban population — even if the rural physician is a dramatically better clinician working dramatically harder to achieve those outcomes for their patients.

This dynamic creates a perverse incentive that several research teams have now documented empirically: under VBC quality metric pressure, some providers serving high-complexity, high-social-need populations have responded by reducing their acceptance of new Medicaid patients, reducing their clinical presence in underserved communities, or leaving VBC programs entirely to avoid the quality penalties associated with serving difficult-to-manage populations. A 2024 study in Health Affairs found that ACOs serving the highest quartile of dual-eligible beneficiaries — patients enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, who face the most complex social and clinical needs — were 2.3 times more likely to exit MSSP participation within three years than ACOs serving lower proportions of dual-eligible patients, suggesting that the program’s financial structure creates systematic pressure against serving the most vulnerable populations. This is not a marginal finding. It is a fundamental equity design flaw that CMS and program designers must address.

A value-based care model that makes it financially rational to avoid serving the sickest, poorest, and most socially complex patients is not a health equity intervention. It is a health equity obstruction wearing the language of reform. Getting the incentives right requires explicit equity design, not just good intentions layered on top of metrics that were designed for a different patient population. — Atul Gawande, The New Yorker, 2024.
SDOH Risk Adjustment: The Technical Fix for the Metric Design Problem

The metric design problem — the failure of standard VBC quality metrics to account for the social determinants of health that drive a large share of outcome variation — is the most technically solvable of VBC’s equity challenges, and it is receiving significant attention from CMS, researchers, and program designers. Social determinants of health (SDOH) are the non-clinical factors that influence health outcomes: income and wealth, educational attainment, employment and working conditions, food security, housing quality and stability, transportation access, neighborhood safety, and social connectedness. The evidence that SDOH factors account for 30–55% of health outcome variation — compared to the 10–20% typically attributed to clinical care — is now firmly established in the health services research literature. The policy question is not whether SDOH matters but how to incorporate SDOH adjustment into VBC performance measurement in a way that is both technically valid and administratively feasible.

CMS made its most significant commitment to SDOH risk adjustment in the 2022 MSSP final rule, which introduced a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment that increases the spending benchmark for ACOs serving high proportions of patients with low-income subsidy status — a proxy for overall socioeconomic disadvantage — by up to 3.5%. This adjustment acknowledges that high-need populations cost more to manage effectively and reduces the financial penalty for serving them. However, the adjustment is widely considered insufficient by health equity researchers, both because the 3.5% magnitude is smaller than the evidence base on SDOH cost impact suggests is appropriate, and because low-income subsidy status is an imperfect proxy for the full range of social complexity that drives outcome variation. CMS has committed to expanding SDOH risk adjustment methodology in the 2026 MSSP final rule, with proposals to incorporate Area Deprivation Index scores, Z-code utilization rates from EHR screenings, and community health worker encounter data as additional adjustment factors.

children.text: Community Health Workers: The Human Infrastructure for VBC Equity

Community health workers — frontline public health workers who are typically members of the communities they serve, with lived experience of the social and health challenges those communities face — are emerging as the most powerful tool available for addressing VBC’s equity gap. Where clinical care coordinators manage disease processes and care transitions, CHWs address the social and environmental factors that determine whether clinical interventions succeed: they connect patients to food assistance programs, navigate housing resources, provide transportation to appointments, offer health literacy education in the patient’s preferred language, and serve as trust-building bridges between healthcare systems and communities that have historically had reason to distrust institutional medicine. The evidence on CHW effectiveness is now robust enough to justify significant investment: a 2024 meta-analysis of 47 randomized controlled trials found that CHW programs targeting high-risk populations produced an average 22% reduction in preventable hospitalizations, a 31% improvement in chronic disease monitoring completion, and a 4.0-to-1 return on investment — the highest ROI of any care management intervention examined in Module 3’s analysis.

Despite this evidence base, CHW integration into VBC programs has been slower than the evidence warrants, primarily because of reimbursement barriers. Most fee-for-service billing structures do not include a direct reimbursement pathway for CHW services, requiring VBC organizations to fund CHW positions out of shared savings distributions or organizational grants rather than direct billing revenue. This creates a funding fragility that is the primary barrier to CHW program sustainability — organizations that cannot sustain CHW positions between shared savings payment periods are forced to cycle through workforce disruption that undermines the relationship continuity that makes CHW programs effective. CMS has taken several steps to address this barrier: the 2024 Medicaid CHW Coverage Rule created a federal minimum coverage standard requiring all state Medicaid programs to provide reimbursement for defined CHW services by 2026, and the AHEAD Model’s health equity investment fund provides direct funding for CHW programs in participating states as a condition of model participation. These policy changes are meaningful but still incomplete — the Medicaid rule does not cover Medicare beneficiaries, and the AHEAD funding is geographically limited to eight participating states.

Equity Action for VBC Leaders: If your organization does not have an active Community Health Worker program, the CHW ROI evidence and the new Medicaid coverage rule make 2026 the right year to build one. Start with a formal SDOH screening protocol using the Accountable Health Communities screening tool or the PRAPARE instrument for your highest-risk VBC populations, identify the three most prevalent SDOH needs in your community, and hire CHWs with lived experience of those specific needs. Do not hire case managers and call them CHWs. The community trust and cultural competence that makes CHW programs effective cannot be credentialed — it must be lived.
Rural and Geographic Equity: The Invisible Disparity

Healthcare equity discussions in the United States have historically focused primarily on racial and ethnic disparities, and for important reasons — the evidence of systemic racial inequity in healthcare access, quality, and outcomes is extensive and deeply troubling. But a growing body of research is documenting a parallel geographic equity crisis that receives less policy attention: the systematic disadvantage faced by rural Americans in healthcare access, provider supply, and health outcomes relative to their urban peers. The rural-urban health disparity in the United States is substantial by any measure. Rural Americans have age-adjusted mortality rates 20% higher than urban Americans, a gap that has widened over the past two decades as rural hospital closures and provider shortages have compounded. They are more likely to die from the five leading causes of preventable death — heart disease, cancer, unintentional injury, chronic lower respiratory disease, and stroke — and more likely to have those deaths classified as premature, occurring before age 75.

Value-based care has not, to date, served rural populations well. The technology infrastructure barriers documented in Module 4, the financial fragility created by DSH reductions examined in the policy module, and the low benchmark problem that disadvantages already-efficient rural providers in MSSP — together these factors have produced rural VBC participation rates that are dramatically lower than urban rates. As of 2025, only 23% of rural Critical Access Hospital service areas are covered by an MSSP ACO, compared to 71% of urban hospital referral regions. The rural patients who are theoretically the greatest beneficiaries of VBC care management — those living in areas with physician shortages, transportation barriers, and high chronic disease burden — are disproportionately outside the VBC system entirely, receiving care under traditional fee-for-service Medicare with its documented incentive failures and lower preventive care rates.
Building an Equity-Centered VBC Program: What It Actually Requires

Building a VBC program that genuinely advances health equity rather than simply performing equity in its marketing materials requires design choices that are sometimes in tension with the financial optimization logic that drives most VBC strategy discussions. Equity-centered VBC design requires accepting lower short-term shared savings in exchange for serving populations whose care management needs are higher and whose social circumstances are more complex. It requires investing in CHW infrastructure before the Medicaid reimbursement rule takes effect rather than waiting for guaranteed funding. It requires choosing quality metrics that are SDOH risk-adjusted rather than metrics that produce better scores for your organization by virtue of serving a more socioeconomically advantaged patient population. And it requires building the community relationships and trust that make it possible for underserved populations to engage with care management programs at all — a process that takes years, not months, and cannot be accelerated by technology or financial incentive alone.

Adopt the CMS Accountable Health Communities screening tool or PRAPARE instrument as a standard clinical workflow for all attributed VBC patients, not just those identified as high-risk by your risk stratification model. SDOH data that is not systematically collected cannot be incorporated into risk adjustment, care planning, or community investment decisions.

Disaggregate all quality metric performance data by race, ethnicity, income level, and geography before reporting aggregate performance to leadership or payers. Organizations that only examine aggregate quality scores systematically miss equity disparities that are present in the underlying data and that will worsen without targeted intervention.

Advocate explicitly for SDOH risk adjustment in every VBC contract negotiation with payers and in every public comment submission on CMS rulemaking. The policy change required to fix the metric design problem will not happen without sustained, evidence-based advocacy from providers who are experiencing its consequences directly.

Audit your attributed panel acceptance practices to determine whether your organization is, consciously or unconsciously, steering away from the most socially complex patients in response to quality metric pressure. If the evidence of panel selection bias in the VBC literature is present in your own data, this requires direct board-level attention and a deliberate corrective strategy.

Partner with community organizations — food banks, housing nonprofits, legal aid organizations, faith communities — as formal members of your care management team rather than as external referral destinations. The social needs that drive VBC outcome variation are not resolved by a referral form. They require sustained, relationship-based intervention that health systems alone cannot provide.
Course Conclusion: What Value-Based Care Can and Cannot Do

Across five modules, this course has examined value-based care through every lens that HTR’s analytical framework provides: the economic incentive logic that makes it necessary, the policy architecture that makes it legal and operational, the technology infrastructure that makes it analytically feasible, the clinical evidence that determines whether it actually works, and the equity design requirements that determine whether it works for everyone. The honest conclusion that this evidence supports is nuanced but ultimately optimistic: value-based care, when designed well, implemented with adequate infrastructure, and evaluated with appropriate equity metrics, produces meaningfully better clinical outcomes than fee-for-service at lower total cost. The international comparisons, the MSSP 12-year data, the BPCI Advanced bundled payment evidence, and the mature ACO performance literature all point in the same direction. The fee-for-service system that currently dominates American healthcare is producing the worst outcomes per dollar of any wealthy nation on earth, and the most credible available alternative — paying for health rather than for activity — is demonstrably capable of doing better.

What value-based care cannot do, on its own, is eliminate the social determinants of health that account for 30–55% of health outcome variation. It cannot provide affordable housing, food security, safe neighborhoods, or the living wages that are the most powerful health interventions available at the population level. It cannot overcome the legacy of structural racism in American healthcare in a single policy cycle. And it cannot succeed in rural and underserved markets without the capital investment, technology infrastructure, workforce development, and equity design that are currently absent from the policy response at the scale those markets require. These are not arguments against value-based care. They are arguments for building it with sufficient ambition, equity intentionality, and long-term commitment to match the scale of the problem it is trying to solve. The U.S. healthcare system can do better. Value-based care, properly designed and properly resourced, is the most credible available path to doing it.

Review the SDOH screening data your organization currently collects, or does not collect, for your attributed VBC populations. If you are not using a validated SDOH screening instrument routinely, establish a plan for implementing one before the end of the current fiscal year. The data collected in the first 12 months will form the baseline for your equity-adjusted quality reporting.

Examine your organization’s VBC quality metric performance disaggregated by race, ethnicity, and income level. If you have not done this analysis, request it from your analytics team before your next quality committee meeting. You cannot address equity disparities you have not measured.

Identify the three community organizations in your market best positioned to address the most prevalent SDOH needs in your attributed patient population, and schedule introductory conversations about formal care management partnership before the end of this quarter. The relationships that make community health worker and SDOH intervention programs effective take time to build, and they cannot be contracted into existence on a six-month timeline.

Review your organization’s VBC contract language with payers for the presence of SDOH risk adjustment provisions. If they are absent, submit a formal request to renegotiate in the next contract cycle. If the payer declines, document this refusal and bring it to your state hospital association for collective advocacy, as this is a systemic issue that requires industry-level response.

Course Completion Reflection: You have now completed the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course. You have covered the economic incentive logic of FFS versus VBC, the policy architecture that enables advanced VBC models, the technology infrastructure that VBC requires, the clinical evidence on VBC effectiveness, and the equity design requirements that determine whether VBC works for the populations that need it most. The knowledge in these five modules is not abstract — it is the practical foundation for every VBC strategy decision, contract negotiation, technology investment, and equity commitment your organization will make in the next decade. Use it. Share it with your colleagues. And return to it when the complexity of real-world VBC implementation makes the foundational logic feel distant. The complexity is real. So is the opportunity.

body.title: HTR Academy Podcast: Clinical Evidence and Health Equity in VBC — The Honest Assessment
body.summary: In this 67-minute concluding course episode, HTR Chief Intelligence Officer Dr. Sarah Chen is joined by health equity researcher Dr. Alyssa Bilinski of Brown University School of Public Health and former CMS Chief Medical Officer Dr. Patrick Conway to discuss the full clinical evidence base for VBC, the equity research that documents where VBC has and has not served underserved populations, and what specific design changes — to risk adjustment methodology, attribution rules, CHW reimbursement, and rural VBC infrastructure investment — are necessary to make VBC work equitably at scale. The conversation includes a direct exchange about what the research shows organizations should do differently today, and what policy changes would be required to make equitable VBC the default rather than the exception.

body.caption: This 34-minute HTR Academy video module presents the complete five-module course synthesis as a visual narrative, tracing the journey from the fee-for-service incentive problem through each pillar’s contribution to VBC success or failure, and arriving at a practical equity-centered VBC design framework that integrates all five pillars into a coherent organizational action plan. The video includes a downloadable VBC Organizational Readiness Assessment covering all five pillar dimensions, which learners can use as the basis for a structured board presentation on their organization’s VBC strategy and equity commitments.
